title: Masei: one date of death (Numbers 33:38)
hook: the only death the Torah dates exactly is Aaron's

segments.voice: Yesterday, Masei, the journeys, with every stop on the road named, even the forgettable ones. Your line was every stop counts. Which places from your life did you remember? Day four hundred seventy-seven.

Some dates live in your phone's calendar. Others live in your body. You feel them coming before you check: the week your father died, the day the house burned, the anniversary nobody else remembers. Many families keep those dates carefully, year after year. In the middle of yesterday's long list of campsites, the Torah stops. Between one station and the next, it pauses for a death. And it does something it does for no one else: it gives the exact date.
screen: `DATES THAT LIVE IN THE BODY.` → `THE LIST STOPS FOR A DEATH.` → `THE EXACT DATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the Lord's command and died there, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel came out of Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month. Then: Aaron was a hundred and twenty-three years old when he died on Mount Hor. Year, month, day and age. Readers have long noticed that this is the only death in the Torah given a full date like this. Even Moses' death, at the end of Deuteronomy, comes without a date. The rabbis later worked out a traditional date for Moses, the seventh of Adar, by calculating from other verses, but the Torah itself doesn't say. For Aaron, it does. The fifth month in the Torah's counting is the month later called Av. So Aaron died on the first of Av, the start of the saddest month of the Jewish year. The Torah had already told the story of his death back in Chukat; here it marks the day. Why? The text doesn't explain. But Jewish life has kept the instinct. The anniversary of a death, by the Hebrew calendar, is called a yahrzeit, a Yiddish word meaning a year's time. On that day many Jews light a candle that burns for a whole day, say the mourner's Kaddish, give charity, and sometimes study in the person's memory. Some communities mark Aaron's own yahrzeit on the first of Av. A death is not just an event in the story; it's a day that comes back, and the Torah gives the first one.
screen: `THE FORTIETH YEAR, FIFTH MONTH, FIRST DAY.` · `NO DATE FOR MOSES IN THE TORAH.` · `THE FIRST OF AV.` · `YAHRZEIT: A YEAR'S TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark a date that matters to you. Settle, and breathe. Think of a date that holds someone: the day a grandparent died, the day a friend was born, the day you got sober, the day a child came home. Picture that person or that moment. If you keep a calendar, decide to put the date in it, so it comes back each year. If you pray, you might think of them by name when it comes. If not, simply hold them for a few breaths now. Stay with them until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Masei. The journeys. In the middle of the list, the Torah stops to give one exact date of death: Aaron's, on the first of Av.
Your line: dates are remembered. Today, put one date that matters into your calendar as a yearly reminder, and add the name it belongs to. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

what a scholar hears: Numbers 33:38 dates it to 1 Av in the fortieth year; Moses' traditional date, 7 Adar, is derived in the Talmud (Kiddushin 38a), not stated in the Torah.
